1. Executive Summary & Problem Landscape

Water-borne diseases—predominantly diarrhea, cholera, typhoid, and hepatitis A—present a severe, recurring mortality burden across rural and tribal belts in India, most acutely throughout the Northeastern Region (NER). Fragile riverine topography, unsealed community borewells, open drainage runoff, and severe monsoon inundations regularly trigger microbial and chemical infiltration into primary drinking water sources.

Currently, public health management functions in a reactive posture: disease outbreaks are identified only after rural Primary Health Centres (PHCs) experience an influx of acutely ill patients. Due to mountainous terrain and isolated transit corridors, medical and chlorination responses arrive days or weeks late, allowing localized water contamination to multiply into community-wide epidemics.

The Critical Surveillance Bottleneck
Conventional microbiological lab testing requires physical sample carriage and 24–72 hours of culturing. AarogyaJal replaces this lagging model with an integrated early warning paradigm combining continuous physical-chemical telemetry (pH, Turbidity, TDS, Temp, Level, DO, Volatile Gases), rapid weekly field test strips (E. coli / Coliforms), and community syndromic reporting via ASHA health workers.

Deploying continuous water surveillance across rugged, low-resource terrain requires an explicit engineering compromise between measurement accuracy, capital cost, and maintenance tolerance.

24/7 continuous telemetry of pH, Level, TDS, Temp, Turbidity, DO, and headspace gases.

3.1 Sensor Modality Trade-Offs: Servicing Tolerance vs. Budget

The central architectural dilemma in environmental monitoring is: How much manual servicing can this deployment tolerate vs. budget? In rural Northeastern India, where nodes are hours away from district centers, automated unattended reliability is paramount.

ISE (Ion-Selective) Drift-Prone
Pros: Cheap and simple for specific ions (Nitrate/Fluoride).
Cons: Severe calibration drift; highly sensitive to ionic interference. Requires recurring calibration against known chemical standards, making unattended rural operation fragile.
Wet-Chemical Analyzers Reagent-Heavy
Pros: Gold-standard lab accuracy in the field.
Cons: Consumes liquid reagents. Requires a trained field technician for periodic refills and pump maintenance. Fails the "install-and-forget" requirement in remote tribal terrain.
Optical / UV Absorption High CapEx
Pros: Drift-free, highly accurate, low ongoing maintenance.
Cons: Prohibitively expensive per unit (₹40,000–₹1,50,000+ per probe). Cannot scale across thousands of rural panchayats with limited public health budgets.
AarogyaJal's Winning Design Decision: Solid-State Core + Surrogate AI Modeling
Instead of fragile wet-chemical reagents or cost-prohibitive UV probes, AarogyaJal deploys robust, solid-state sensors (**pH, Water Level, TDS, Temperature, Turbidity, DO**) paired with periodic weekly manual paper test strips. This eliminates recurring technician reagent costs while retaining maximum field durability.

3.2 Real-Time Surrogates: BOD & Algal Bloom (Chlorophyll-a)

  • Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD): BOD cannot be sensed directly in real-time because standard BOD₅ requires a 5-day biological incubation period. AarogyaJal circumvents this by computing an Inferred Organic Load Surrogate: combining real-time Dissolved Oxygen (DO) depletion rates, turbidity spikes, and water temperature into an ML-derived proxy for sudden organic/septic contamination.
  • Chlorophyll-a (Algal Bloom Proxy): Measured via fluorescence sensors. Evaluated as an optional Phase-2 add-on for open surface reservoirs and community harvesting ponds, but excluded from base drinking water nodes to preserve sub-₹5,500 unit economics.
  • The Fundamental Four Continuous Baseline: pH (chemical stability), Water Level (tank volume/sudden drainage), TDS/Conductivity (salinity/dissolved ionic intrusion), and Temperature (thermal correction & bacterial kinetic modeling).

Mass Deployability & Fiscal Sustainability
At an average node cost of ₹5,500 (~$65 USD), an entire district water surveillance network spanning 50 critical points of interest (handpumps, storage tanks, and riverbanks) can be outfitted for under ₹2.75 Lakh—less than the acquisition cost of a single municipal-grade SCADA monitoring station.

4.1 Edge Energy Budget, Harvesting & Anti-Fouling Architecture

  • Low-Power Duty Cycle: ESP32 firmware executes a 55-second deep sleep cycle (<15 µA quiescent draw) followed by a 5-second burst sensing, analog-to-digital averaging, and MQTT transmission phase. Average operational consumption is constrained to ~20 mA at 3.3V.
  • Monsoon Solar Power Budget: A compact 5W–10W monocrystalline solar panel produces 18–25 Wh daily under normal diffuse sunlight. The edge node consumes approximately 0.48 Wh per 24-hour operating period, providing a ~40× safety multiplier to sustain autonomous operation through 14 consecutive days of heavy overcast monsoonal rains.
  • Anti-Fouling & Electrode Longevity: Alternating current (AC) excitation pulses across TDS/conductivity probes eliminate galvanic polarization, prevent electrode oxidation, and inhibit biological biofilm fouling in stagnant well environments.

5. Target Pilot Deployments: Northeastern Region (NER)

Due to extreme rainfall, seasonal floods, and fragmented healthcare networks, five high-risk pilot sites in the NER have been earmarked to validate sensor performance and predictive outbreak modeling under harsh operating conditions:

1. Majuli, Assam River Island Aquifer
Installation Point: Exit manifold of community handpump near Brahmaputra riverbank.
Risk Vector: Monsoonal river swells cause subsurface silt infiltration and cross-contamination of shallow drinking aquifers.
2. Churachandpur, Manipur Centralized Reservoir
Installation Point: Village-level gravity-fed overhead storage reservoir.
Risk Vector: Centralized distribution point; a single pathogen infiltration instantly contaminates the entire settlement.
3. Tura, Meghalaya Traditional Open Well
Installation Point: Community dug well located in Rongram Block.
Risk Vector: Heavy precipitation causes rapid agricultural and surface runoff into the well, spiking turbidity and fecal coliforms.
4. Aizawl, Mizoram Drainage Discharge
Installation Point: Drain exit point discharging into a community harvesting pond.
Risk Vector: Untreated hillside sewage overflow mixes directly with primary community bathing and utility water.
5. Pasighat, Arunachal Pradesh Borewell Riverbank Infiltration
Installation Point: Community borewell discharge outlet adjacent to the Siang riverbank.
Risk Vector: Frequent flash floods cause backflow and seepage of river silt and untreated surface waste into borewell intake pipes.

8. Outbreak Prediction Engine & Risk Index Formulation

The prediction engine computes a dynamic Outbreak Risk Index (ORI) by fusing physical telemetry deviations, microbiological validations, and localized syndromic health reports:

Algorithmic Formulation: Outbreak Risk Index (ORI)

ORI = w₁ · ΔWQI(t) + w₂ · Biol(t) + w₃ · Σ SymptomCluster(t, r) + w₄ · SeasonRainFactor(t)

Where ΔWQI tracks rate of parameter deviation (pH, Turbidity, DO, TDS); Biol represents positive E. coli strip detection; SymptomCluster aggregates ASHA diarrheal and febrile complaint surges within radius r; and SeasonRainFactor scales risk during peak monsoon flooding. If ORI exceeds 0.75, automated emergency alerts are dispatched.

The AarogyaJal Hardware Differentiation
Existing market hardware falls into two extremes: hyper-expensive municipal SCADA instruments (₹8L–₹35L like YSI and s::can) or intermittent manual testing devices (CLUIX, OmniVis). AarogyaJal creates a new category: an autonomous 24/7 continuous multi-probe array at under ₹5,500 with integrated solar harvesting.
